To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the metabolic syndrome, as well as its components, are associated with anthropometric indices in adolescents, but the most powerful anthropometric indices to predict the metabolic risk are BMI, waist circumference, and WHR, whereas the waist‐to‐height ratio is the most powerful anthropometry to predict the metabolic and inflammatory risk.
the metabolic syndrome and the components of the metabolic syndrome can be predicted in adolescents using anthropometric indices, with waist‐to‐height ratio being the best anthropometric index.
BMI, BMI standard deviation score and waist/height are the strongest predictors of the metabolic risk in children.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following topics:
The metabolic syndrome and its individual components (e.g., obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension) in adolescents.
the development of a model to predict the metabolic risk in children and adolescents based on anthropometric indices.

the following: (i) the relationship between anthropometric indices and metabolic syndrome (MS) in adolescents, (ii) the relationship between the components of the MS and anthropometric indices in adolescents, (iii) the relationship between low‐grade inflammation and anthropometric indices and (iv) the relationship between components of MS and low‐grade inflammatory markers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the waist/height ratio and WHR are the best anthropometric predictors in adolescents.

BMI, BMI standard deviation score and WHR are the best anthropometric indices to predict the metabolic components of the metabolic syndrome, while WHR is the best index to predict the metabolic risk factors and low‐grade inflammatory state in adolescents.

the waist circumference is the most powerful anthropometric index in the diagnosis of the metabolic syndrome in adolescents, while the BMI standard deviation score is the best anthropometric index in predicting the metabolic syndrome components and low‐level inflammation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
anthropometrical indices are useful for screening adolescents for the metabolic syndrome and some of its components.
the metabolic syndrome and most of its components are more strongly related to waist circumference and waist/height index than to BMI and BMI‐SDS.
the waist‐to‐height ratio (WHtR) has the highest predictive power of all the anthropometric indices for the metabolic syndrome in adolescents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
BMI, waist circumference, and waist/height are all good predictors for the metabolic syndrome and for the components of the syndrome in adolescents.

the metabolic syndrome is a complex condition that is not easily predicted by any single measure of adiposity, and that a combination of anthropometric measures is likely required for optimal prediction of the condition.
waist‐to‐height ratio may be a more sensitive indicator of the presence of the metabolic syndrome in adolescents than BMI or waist circumference.
